Photograph: John Sellers Brexit Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit Scale of deportations made public for first time amid criticism of hardline approach to UK citizens Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.16 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 05.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Sweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit. It is the first time the scale of the deportations of citizens who failed to secure residency in Sweden post-Brexit has been made public and comes amid mounting criticism of a cruel and hardline approach to Britons who had chosen to make the country their home before Brexit . Some have been told to go after more than 25 years in the country and even vulnerable elderly people with dementia have been affected. One man was deported even though he had lived in the country since he was 10 years old. Susanna Fonsell, a unit manager and legal expert at the Swedish Migration Agency, told Sverige Radio: “A rejected application does not necessarily result in deportation… and according to the agency statistics, the agency’s rejections of an application for resident status has been accomplished by a deportation decision in only approximately 400 cases,” she told Sweden Radio . The Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, confirmed to the Guardian that 458 British citizens had been deported since Brexit. “According to the agency’s statistics, the Swedish Migration Agency’s rejection of an application for residence status has been accompanied by a deportation decision in only 458 cases,” a spokesperson said. David Milstead, who heads up the 9,000-strong activist group Brits in Sweden, said it was important for Sweden to release full and transparent figures in relation to removals and deportations and their circumstances. “We need to understand exactly what the 458 represents. Does it capture people who gave up and left when they realised their withdrawal agreement application was unlikely to succeed? Does it include people who were refused withdrawal agreement status, subsequently obtained a permit under national law and were only later ordered to leave? “It certainly does not capture people who are currently managing to remain in Sweden on temporary permits, with little certainty about their long-term future.” He said the figures illustrated a “broader problem” in that the data was issued piecemeal and sometimes in an opaque manner. “We still do not have basic published figures showing how many people submitted a missed-deadline application and the fraction of these which succeeded,” he said. The last available data shows that there were 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency, which included family members joining British citizens after the deadline by 2024. Of those, just under 4,000 were rejected, a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%, according to Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) analysis. Deportations are still happening. This week, the Swedish wife of a former business director from Cambridge told how her husband was detained in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a forced removal. She said they had been fighting to overturn the decision by the migration authorities for five years and felt that they had been “hunted” . Earlier this week, the Guardian revealed a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, who had lived in Sweden since he was 10, had been deported , separating him from his wife, Caroline, in Gothenburg, who said people needed to know how Brexit had “crushed families”. View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas, 78, is facing removal from Sweden as a result of its hardline Brexit policy. Photograph: Felix Andler Another woman, 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, has been told to remove herself from the country before next Wednesday . Friends are trying to get an injunction and have appealed to the European Commission for help. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and be “registered on a watchlist” preventing potential entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”. The Swedish Migration Agency told the Guardian it had “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. The Swedish Migration Agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions.” Late applications for post-Brexit residency are allowed under the Brexit withdrawal agreement, both in the EU and the UK, but applicants have to show “reasonable grounds” for missing the deadline. The FCDO has said that “in practice” late applicants in Sweden “are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”. Earlier this week, Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, said his government had followed the rules but that it was willing to look into the matter. “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future,” he said. A spokesperson for the FCDO said: “We continue to raise this with the Swedish authorities and welcome their statement that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so.” Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for Sweden’s opposition Centre party, said the government needed to go much further. He pledged to bring in new laws if his party won power at the next general election to allow British to reapply for post-Brexit residence, saying “a touch of humanity” was needed . (Image: Beth Prodger) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. There was a sobering consensus in the room that Scotland and the wider UK are facing threats from foreign powers that will result in a large-scale conflict in the near future. Military leaders, senior civil servants, defence analysts, academics and industry bosses were among the experts who delivered stark assessments on how geopolitics in 2026 has put the British and western authorities on high alert to potential attacks, especially from Russia . They were among the figures who gathered in central Edinburgh last Thursday to take stock of threats facing Scotland and the UK and to assess current preparations for a large-scale conflict which military chiefs could say could erupt by 2030. The growing threat has led to the Scottish Government becoming involved in developing a new "War Book" with the UK Government which sets the measures that would come into force across the UK in the event of conflict. The aim of the Edinburgh meeting, some of which took place under Chatham House rules, was to achieve a better understanding of Scotland’s importance to UK national security and to understand how the Scottish Government and Westminster can best work together to improve resilience and preparedness for a major conflict either at home or against a Nato ally which would automatically engage the UK because of Nato's collective defence policy. Read More: Scotland to develop 'War Book' with UK amid growing threats Russian spy ship directed lasers at UK military pilots, Defence Secretary says Why is the Russian spy ship Yantar in Scottish waters? Scotland would be a first Russian target, experts warn Should Scots households keep 'war supplies' like Finns? UK lacks plan to defend itself from military attack, say MPs Much of President Vladmir Putin's current campaign, described by some defence experts as a "hybrid war" against Western and Nato nations, has been focused around the "High North" and European states in Russia's vicinity such as Finland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. But the Ministry of Defence has suggested that Britain is in Russia line of sight too with a 30% rise in Russian naval activity around UK waters over the past two years with incidents coming to the public attention. They included the Russian spy ship Yantar which is believed to have been deployed along with a submarine in the Irish Sea to survey the gas pipeline linking Britain and Ireland. The Yantar incident was particularly troubling as it was confirmation that attempts by Russia to sabotage critical subsea infrastructure off Norway and in the Baltic now appeared to be moving towards Britain - and off the Scottish coast in particular. At Thursday's meeting Stewart McDonald, the SNP 's former defence spokesman, who now serves as senior adviser on defence and security at the Dublin-based public affairs firm Fenton Fitzwilliam, where he is part of a pan-European network of people with political, diplomatic, military, and security expertise who advise clients across the continent, set the scene - starting with Scotland's proximity to the Scandinavian states. Former SNP MP Stewart McDonald (Image: Gordon Terris) "Scotland sits across the GIUK gap [the main and most practical gateway for Russia’s Northern Fleet to enter the Atlantic] and we are critical to the UK's ability to watch and defend it," he told the conference, hosted by The D Group consultancy and the British Foreign Policy Group. Mr McDonald underlined that the case needed to be made for Scotland to understand its place in national security "far better than it does, and that this demands a kind of political attention it has lacked since the Scottish Parliament was established in 1999". He listed the UK defence facilities based in Scotland - the Royal Navy's submarine service and the UK's nuclear deterrent which are based on the Clyde, at Faslane and Coulport, the maritime patrol aircraft that watch the North Atlantic, and the Typhoons that intercept Russian aircraft approaching UK airspace from the north, fly from Lossiemouth. " Prestwick Airport, which is owned by the Scottish Government, matters to Nato, to the UK and to Ukraine far beyond what its size as an airport would suggest," he said. "Then there is civilian infrastructure that would be a target in any serious confrontation, some of which is already being probed. The subsea cables and inter-connectors that run between Scotland, Ireland, the Northern Isles and the Faroes come ashore on our coasts. "A large share of the gas that heats British homes arrives at St Fergus in Aberdeenshire. "The North Sea installations, the offshore wind farms now being built at scale, the onshore grid that will carry their power south, the ports that service all of it: this is critical national infrastructure in the formal sense of the term, and Scotland has lots of it. And we know that much of this is of interest to our adversaries." He added: "Indeed when you put the geography and the inventory together, and consider the complex threat picture we face, you arrive at a sobering conclusion. Scotland is both a forward edge of Nato's northern flank and a target for anyone who wants to weaken the alliance below the threshold of war." Read More: Are Scotland's undersea cables safe from Russian sabotage? Scots defence industry 'can benefit' from closer EU UK work Top EU diplomat in Scottish universities Brexit warning Brexit has made Scotland £30 billion a year worse off Keir Starmer says £15bn defence investment plan will prepare UK for war Professor Kristen Harkness, of the School of International Relations at St Andrew's University, warned that Scotland's large coastline and numerous island communities present heightened security risks in terms of potential Russian sabotage of sub sea cables "What is of most concern to Scotland is the intensification of sabotage of European under sea critical infrastructure," she told the gathering. She pointed to a possibility that because Scotland is geographically close to where Russian has been attempting to damage sub sea cables off Norway and in the Baltic, Scotland could be a "target of ease". She added that Scotland was also vulnerable because of its large coastline and island communities heavily dependent on sub sea infrastructure. "We have a lot of islands and a lot of communities on islands and they are all connected through their telecommunications. their power, their internet," she said. "Communities may need to be prepared, particularly island communities, to go for a period of time with power or internet cuts." She said assessments would be needed of how much critical services - including health and education - delivered more often remotely in island communities than on the mainland - are dependent on sub sea infrastructure. "How dependent are our services on sub sea infrastructure that could be damaged in attacks?" she asked. "And this ties back into the issue of resilience and how communities can increase their resilience." War resilience boxes are extra supplies of food, water, blankets, batteries and medicine that (Image: Derek McArthur) Mr McDonald argued that substantially more work needed to be done to improve Scotland's resilience - as he urged the Scottish Government to learn lessons from Sweden, Finland and Norway on how to prepare citizens for a possible attack or war. "The government of Sweden has twice in the last decade sent every household a booklet, under the title 'If Crisis or War Comes', setting out what people should do, what they should have at home and what the state will expect of them in the event of crisis or conflict. "Norway does the same. Finland has built its whole approach to security around the idea that the state, business and the citizen each have a part to play, and runs national defence courses that have put a large share of the country's leaders in every field through the same training. "Nobody in Stockholm, Oslo or Helsinki thinks of this as frightening the public or scaremongering. They think of it as treating people as adults who can be told the truth and asked to prepare." He added: "The conversation with the public about preparedness must take on real urgency. The Nordic governments talk to their citizens about what to do in a crisis as a matter of routine, and the Scottish Government, which already runs most of the services people would turn to, is well placed to do the same. "That means plain guidance, regularly refreshed, on what households should expect and what they should have at home, and a willingness to talk about conflict as well as floods, wildfires and pandemics. It must be a whole-of-society effort beyond just the state."
